If your Apple CarPlay connection drops while you're driving, the problem may not be with your iPhone, cable, or car.

It could instead be caused by radio interference.

A recent Axios report detailed a strange phenomenon in Boston, where CarPlay or Android Auto connections drop when drivers pass through certain stretches of road. Similar 'dead zones' may exist in other cities, but no one has flagged them yet.

CarPlay head units can't process GPS navigation on their own — they maintain a direct Bluetooth or Wi-Fi connection with your iPhone and mirror the display. Everything on screen relies on your phone's internet and GPS satellite signals. When the wireless connection between the head unit and the phone is disrupted, navigation fails and the connection can drop.

The top-liked comment came from Mainframe

In Grapevine, Texas, I know of a specific stretch of road, sandwiched between an oil depot and a nursing home, where every wireless CarPlay system crashes as you drive through. I've tried it with multiple vehicles — a car with factory-equipped wireless CarPlay, a wireless CarPlay adapter, and an aftermarket stereo — and all of them died on this stretch. Some systems recovered automatically after the interference passed; others did not. Even the latest Mercedes-Benz electric vehicle has this issue.

In the last ten years, I've only encountered this situation a handful of times.

Experts note that nearby radio sources — particularly signals in the 2.4GHz band — may be the source of the interference. In Boston's case, suspects could include point-to-point microwave links, broadcast antennas, or unlicensed transmitters.

Most importantly: if you repeatedly lose your CarPlay connection in the same location, you may be driving through an invisible zone of radio interference. The problem may not be fixable, but knowing the cause can save you considerable time — endless troubleshooting and unnecessary repair appointments.
